newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: IBM Microelectronics opens Asia Pacific HQ.
newsitem.headline: IBM Microelectronics opens Asia Pacific HQ.

text.p: IBM Microelectronics, a division of International Business Machines Corp, opened its Asia Pacific headquarters in Singapore on Wednesday.
IBM Microelectronics develops, manufactures and markets semiconductor technologies, product packaging and services.
Until 1992, the company provided products only to IBM divisions. Now, 50 percent of its semiconductor business comes from outside IBM, officials said at the opening of the office.
The regional headquarters will help the company to increase its business in the region, including Japan, they said.

"We expect to grow in this geography ahead of the market place expansion. Between now and the end of the decade, we expect to grow faster than rest of the market," said John Gleason, general manager worldwide marketing and sales.
"The rest of the market growing at a compounded forecast growth of 20 percent," he told reproters

Semiconductor sales in the Asia-Pacific region are forecast at US$75 billion for 1997 -- close to 50 percent of the world market -- and projected to grow to US$139 billion in 2000, said Kenneth Kin, IBM Microelectronics vice president, Asia Pacific. The officials declined to reveal the company's revenue in the region.

They said the microelectronics division was targetting the consumer, communications and data processing markets. It would be developing strategic partnerships with key customers in the region and expand its sales and distributorships in emerging markets like India and China.
Gleason said IBM had a worldwide semiconductor market share of about 2.7-3.0 percent, excluding internal sales.
He said a new joint venture wafer fabrication plant with Toshiba would help to raise the company's market share in 1998.
The U.S.-based plant for eight-inch sub-micron wafers, the raw materials for the production of semiconductors, is scheduled to start operations in the third quarter this year.
It would reach full capacity production in 1998 when it would produce about 1,000 wafers a day for the worldwide market, Gleason said.
